name: Virtue, or its look-alike anti-pattern?
note: The AI-assisted anti-patterns are dangerous because they mimic the virtues — speed looks like skill, confidence like comprehension. The tell is always whether a committed standard and real understanding sit behind the behaviour.

items.prompt: An engineer ships a feature in 20 minutes with AI. Virtue or anti-pattern?
candidates: Can't tell from speed alone — a virtue if they clarified, committed a standard, and verified against it in those 20 minutes; the velocity trap if 'done' just means 'the demo ran.' The tell is the committed standard, not the clock
Anti-pattern — shipping that fast is always reckless
Virtue — as long as the tests pass
items.correct: Can't tell from speed alone — a virtue if they clarified, committed a standard, and verified against it in those 20 minutes; the velocity trap if 'done' just means 'the demo ran.' The tell is the committed standard, not the clock
items.explanation: Velocity is neutral. Governed velocity (speed with a committed standard and verification) is the virtue; ungoverned velocity is the trap. The look-alikes differ only by whether a standard exists behind the speed.
items.principle: Speed is neither virtue nor vice — the committed standard behind it is.

items.prompt: A candidate tries six prompt variations until the output passes the tests. Virtue or anti-pattern?
candidates: Prompt theater if the tests were the handed-down ones and no standard was committed first — they're tuning until the failure hides; it would be steering if they were iterating toward invariants they had already preregistered
Virtue — persistence in prompting shows skill
Anti-pattern — you should never iterate on a prompt
items.correct: Prompt theater if the tests were the handed-down ones and no standard was committed first — they're tuning until the failure hides; it would be steering if they were iterating toward invariants they had already preregistered
items.explanation: Iterating toward a committed spec is steering — each attempt is measured against a standard you set. Iterating until handed-down tests go green is prompt theater: the failure gets hidden, not fixed.
items.principle: Iterating toward your committed standard is steering; iterating until the test goes green is theater.

items.prompt: The AI's output contradicts your own calculation. The candidate goes with the AI 'because it's usually right.' Read?
candidates: Automation bias — deferring to the tool over your own check is the failure; the right move is to resolve the contradiction (re-derive, test it), not to assume the AI wins. Justified trust comes after checking, not instead of it
Reasonable — modern models are right more often than people
Always distrust the AI and use your own answer instead
Fine, as long as the AI explained its reasoning
items.correct: Automation bias — deferring to the tool over your own check is the failure; the right move is to resolve the contradiction (re-derive, test it), not to assume the AI wins. Justified trust comes after checking, not instead of it
items.explanation: Automation bias is trusting the automation over contradicting evidence. The cure isn't blanket distrust — it's resolving the conflict with a check, so trust (when it comes) is earned rather than assumed.
items.principle: When the AI and your check disagree, resolve it — don't defer to the tool's reputation.
